moments.title: Why precision matters
moments.text: Questions may require a specified number of decimal places or significant figures. Keep the requested form in mind when reporting a final answer.

moments.title: Start with a large number
moments.text: The presenter uses $62562.3418$ to compare rounding to two decimal places and three significant figures.

moments.title: Round to two decimal places
moments.text: Keep the hundredths digit and inspect the next digit. Since it is 1, the result is $62562.34$.

moments.title: The first discarded digit
moments.text: A first discarded digit of 0 to 4 leaves the last retained digit unchanged; 5 to 9 rounds it up.

moments.title: Counting significant figures
moments.text: Count from the first nonzero digit. Zeros inside a number can be significant; leading zeros are not.

moments.title: Round to three significant figures
moments.text: The first three digits are 6, 2 and 5. The next digit is 6, so $62562.3418$ becomes $62600$ to 3 significant figures.

moments.title: Why the final zeros appear
moments.text: The zeros in $62600$ preserve place value. Standard form $6.26\times10^4$ also communicates the three significant figures clearly.

moments.title: A small number: decimal places
moments.text: The second number is $0.005826$. To two decimal places the result is $0.01$, since the third decimal digit is 5.

moments.title: A small number: significant figures
moments.text: Ignore the leading zeros; the first three significant digits are 5, 8 and 2. The next digit is 6, giving $0.00583$.

moments.title: Apply rounding in a question
moments.text: The presenter moves from standalone examples to a volume result that must be given at two levels of precision.

moments.title: Volume to two decimal places
moments.text: For the volume result $369.408$, the third decimal digit is 8, so rounding to two decimal places gives $369.41$.

moments.title: Volume to three significant figures
moments.text: The first three significant digits of $369.408$ are 3, 6 and 9. The next digit is 4, so the result is $369$.

notes.title: Zeros and stated precision
notes.text: A final zero in a whole number may be a placeholder, but it can also represent a stated level of precision. Without more information the number of significant figures may be ambiguous.
notes.write: Use standard form to make the precision explicit: $6.26\times10^4$ has three significant figures.

moments.title: Comparing an estimate with an exact value
moments.text: Percentage error expresses the size of the error relative to the exact value.

moments.title: Estimate and actual count
moments.text: The presenter estimates 450 jelly beans when the actual number is 500, then asks for the percentage error.

moments.title: Percentage-error formula
moments.text: $\left|\frac{\text{approximate}-\text{exact}}{\text{exact}}\right|\times100\%$; the absolute value makes the reported error nonnegative.

moments.title: Substitute the values
moments.text: Put 450 in the approximate-value position and 500 in both exact-value positions.

moments.title: Find the percentage error
moments.text: The signed fraction is $-0.1$; its absolute value is $0.1$, or 10%.

moments.title: Compare estimates
moments.text: A smaller percentage error indicates an estimate closer to the exact value relative to that exact value.

moments.title: Apply the formula in a question
moments.text: The presenter switches to an estimate of $0.03$ and an exact value of $0.0375$.

notes.title: Illustrative error estimates
notes.text: The presenter informally suggests possible errors for estimates of 490 and 750 when the exact count is 500. Those suggested percentages are not calculated.

ican.text: I can round a value to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures, including very small values.
I can use standard form to show the intended number of significant figures.
I can find the lower and upper bounds implied by a rounded measurement and use appropriate inequality symbols.
I can calculate absolute, relative and percentage error when the exact value is known and nonzero.
I can interpret the size of an error in context and retain sufficient precision in intermediate working.
I can use bounds to find a maximum percentage error in a calculated quantity.

ku.text: Decimal places are counted from the decimal point. Significant figures begin at the first nonzero digit and then include zeros between significant digits.
Round using the first discarded digit: 0 to 4 leaves the final retained digit unchanged; 5 to 9 increases it by one. A carry can change earlier digits: $9.995$ to 3 significant figures is $10.0$.

Trailing zeros after a decimal point can communicate precision: $2.50$ has 3 significant figures. A whole number such as $2500$ can be ambiguous without additional information; $2.50\times10^3$ makes 3 significant figures explicit.

For a nonnegative measurement rounded to the nearest unit $h$ and reported as $a>0$, its bounds are $a-h/2\le x<a+h/2$ under the usual half-up convention. Restrict the interval further if the context requires it.
The absolute error is $|\text{approximate}-\text{exact}|$. Relative error divides the absolute error by the magnitude of the nonzero exact value; percentage error multiplies that ratio by $100\%$.
Carry unrounded values through a calculation and round the final result as requested. The difference between two rounded values can amplify a small intermediate rounding error.

For a derived quantity such as $A=\pi r^2$, first find the possible bounds of the exact quantity from the measurement bounds. Compare the estimate with the exact value at the relevant endpoints; percentage error divides by the exact value.

terms.text: Count places to the right of the decimal point and use the next digit to decide whether to round up.
Start at the first nonzero digit. Keep the requested number of significant digits and use the next digit.
Give the complete interval of values consistent with the stated rounding, including which endpoints are included.
Identify the approximate and exact values, show the difference relative to the exact value, then report a percentage.

formula.text: Percentage error: $\left|\dfrac{\text{approximate value}-\text{exact value}}{\text{exact value}}\right|\times100\%$, for a nonzero exact value.

worked.prompt: A metal rod has an exact length of $12.376$ cm. A student records the length as $12.4$ cm, rounded to the nearest $0.1$ cm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: State the interval of lengths that would round to $12.4$ cm.
parts.a: Half the rounding unit is $0.05$ cm. Therefore $12.35\le L<12.45$ cm.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the percentage error in the recorded length, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: State whether the recorded length is an underestimate or an overestimate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: A different measurement gives a circle's radius as 2.5 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm. Using the calculated area $6.25\pi$ as the estimate, find the maximum percentage error relative to the exact area.
parts.a: The exact radius is in $[2.45,2.55)$ cm, so the exact area lies in $[6.0025\pi,6.5025\pi)$. At the lower bound, the percentage error is $\frac{6.25-6.0025}{6.0025}\times100\%=4.12328\ldots\%$. The error toward the upper bound approaches $\frac{6.5025-6.25}{6.5025}\times100\%\approx3.88\%$, which is smaller. The maximum is therefore $4.12\%$ to 3 significant figures.

kq.q: Why are the final zeros in $6.26\times10^4$ more informative than those in $62600$?
kq.model: The coefficient explicitly contains three significant figures. The whole-number form alone does not distinguish precision from place-value placeholders.

kq.q: Why is the upper bound for a value rounded to $12.4$ cm normally excluded?
kq.model: With the stated half-up rounding convention, $12.45$ cm rounds to $12.5$ cm, not $12.4$ cm.

kq.q: Why can two errors of the same absolute size have different percentage errors?
kq.model: Percentage error compares the error with the exact value. The same absolute error is a larger fraction of a smaller nonzero exact value.

kq.q: Why does a nonnegative percentage error not indicate whether an estimate was too high or too low?
kq.model: The absolute value removes the sign. Compare the estimate with the exact value separately to state direction.
